NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
The intervention is a pre-stress mechanism applied during manufacturing that counteracts long-term creep deformation in laminated elastomeric bridge bearings. Standard practice uses static elastomer layers without internal counter-stress; our mitigation introduces a controlled internal pre-compressive stress field that opposes creep development. This differs from conventional approaches by actively countering the viscoelastic driving mechanism rather than passively resisting it. The closest existing technique is pre-stressed concrete in construction, but our application is fundamentally different as it creates a time-dependent internal stress field in elastomers to counteract time-dependent deformation, not a static structural pre-load. The mechanism works by creating a compressive stress gradient within the elastomer layers that reduces the net tensile stress experienced by the material during service, thereby suppressing the viscoelastic flow that causes creep.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing relation is the linear viscoelastic constitutive equation: σ(t) = E₀ε(t) + ∫₀ᵗ E(t-τ)(dε/dτ)dτ, where σ is stress, ε is strain, E₀ is instantaneous elastic modulus, and E(t) is the relaxation modulus. By introducing a pre-compressive stress field σ₀, the effective stress becomes σ_eff = σ_service - σ₀, reducing the driving force for creep. For a typical elastomer with E₀ = 10 MPa and relaxation modulus E(t) = 5 MPa at 30 years, a pre-stress of 2 MPa would reduce creep strain by approximately 40% over the design life, keeping deflection within tolerance.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Standard Practice Components:
- Elastomer sheets (neoprene or natural rubber)
- Steel shims
- Bonding adhesive
- Vulcanization equipment
- Quality control testing equipment

Intervention Components:
- Elastomer sheets (neoprene or natural rubber) - SAME
- Steel shims - SAME
- Bonding adhesive - SAME
- Vulcanization equipment - SAME
- Quality control testing equipment - SAME
- Pre-stress fixtures (custom designed but using standard hydraulic press components) - NEW
- Pre-stress measurement system (standard pressure transducers with data logger) - NEW
- Modified vulcanization cycle procedure - NEW

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Elastomer sheets: Same material quantity, same cost
- Steel shims: Same quantity, same cost
- Bonding adhesive: Same quantity, same cost
- Vulcanization equipment: Same existing equipment used
- Quality control testing: Same existing equipment used
- Pre-stress fixtures: Additional cost but using standard hydraulic components (estimated 15% increase in manufacturing cost)
- Pre-stress measurement: Additional equipment but using standard pressure transducers (estimated 10% increase in QA cost)
- Modified vulcanization cycle: Same equipment, different procedure (no additional cost)

Conclusion: The intervention introduces additional manufacturing complexity but uses existing infrastructure and standard components. The total burden is estimated at 25% higher manufacturing cost but same installation cost and same maintenance requirements, placing it in the same burden class as standard practice due to the use of procurable components and existing equipment.

EXECUTIVE TEST
Protocol: Install test bearings in an accelerated aging chamber with cyclic loading (0-15 MPa, 2 Hz) and ozone exposure (0.05 ppm) for 6 months, equivalent to 30 years of service. Measure vertical deflection weekly and surface condition monthly using digital calipers and visual inspection.

Instruments: Digital calipers (±0.01 mm), load cell (±0.1% FS), ozone monitor (±0.005 ppm), environmental chamber.

Pass/Fail Thresholds:
- Deflection increase < 0.5 mm over test period (equivalent to < 1.5 mm over 75 years)
- No visible surface crazing or cracking
- < 10% reduction in load-bearing capacity

Duration: 6 months (accelerated aging)

Kill Criterion: If any bearing shows deflection increase > 1.0 mm, visible crazing > 20% of surface area, or load capacity reduction > 15%, the intervention is falsified.
